steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper presenting GlotScript, a resource and a tool for identifying the writing system (script) of text in low resource languages. Motivate why script identification is useful, contrast it with language identification, and finish with a list of contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- What script identification is
- Why it is useful for low resource languages (corpus quality control, tokenizer analysis)
- Language identification as an alternative, and why it falls short
- GlotScript: resource and tool
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- What script identification is
  - goal: automatically identify writing system / script a text is written in
  - we call this "script identification"
- Why useful for low resource languages
  - corpus compilation: quality control, drop texts in scripts not used for the language
  - tokenizer of LM for low resource languages: analyze learned vocabulary -> how well a script is represented -> indication of how well languages in that script are represented
- Language identification as alternative
  - also usable for quality control and vocab analysis
  - but LID for low resource languages: high error rates (cite)
  - reasons: data scarcity, high variability in orthography, genres, domains
  - script ID much higher accuracy -> useful when no reliable LID
- GlotScript
  - resource + tool for low resource identification of writing systems = low resource script identification
- Contributions
  - (i) GlotScript-R: comprehensive resource, attested writing systems <-> language varieties; released to community
  - (ii) GlotScript-T: tool, covers all 161 scripts in Unicode 15.0; computes script distribution for any input text; ISO 15924 codes; no such tool available (to our knowledge)
  - (iii) corpus cleaning with GlotScript-T and -R; quality of existing low resource corpora can be improved
  - (iv) tokenization analysis of LLMs (GPT-4, Falcon, Llama2) with GlotScript-T; insights on LLM coverage / lack of coverage of low resource languages

We want to automatically identify the writing system, or script, that a given text is written in. We call this automatic identification of scripts script identification. Script identification is useful when doing research and building technology for low resource languages. For example, when a corpus is compiled for a low resource language, script identification can be used for quality control, because texts that are written in scripts that are not used for the language can be removed. steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
We want to automatically identify the writing system, or script, that a given text is written in. We call this automatic identification of scripts script identification. Script identification is useful when doing research and building technology for low resource languages. For example, when a corpus is compiled for a low resource language, script identification can be used for quality control, because texts that are written in scripts that are not used for the language can be removed. In a similar way, when the tokenizer of a language model for low resource languages is trained, developers can analyze the learned token vocabulary to see how well a script is represented, and this is an indication of how well the languages written in that script are represented.

Language identification is an alternative to script identification in these low resource scenarios, since language identification can also be used for quality control and to analyze language model vocabularies. But language identification has high error rates for low resource languages. Existing tools identify many low resource languages poorly, because there is not much data and there is a lot of variability in orthography, genres and domains. Script identification on the other hand can be done with much higher accuracy, so it is a useful functionality when there is no reliable language identification for many low resource languages.

In this paper we present GlotScript, which is a resource and a tool for identifying writing systems for low resource languages, i.e., low resource script identification.

Our contributions are the following. (i) We put together and organize GlotScript-R, which is a comprehensive resource for script identification that associates attested writing systems with language varieties. We make the resource available to the community. (ii) We publish GlotScript-T, which is a script identification tool that covers all 161 scripts in Unicode 15.0. It computes the distribution of scripts for any input text. The scripts are identified by their ISO 15924 codes. As far as we know, there is no such tool available right now. (iii) We show the benefits of GlotScript-T and GlotScript-R for cleaning corpora, and we show that script identification can improve the quality of existing low resource corpora. (iv) We use GlotScript-T to analyze the tokenization of large language models (LLMs), including GPT-4, Falcon and Llama2. This analysis gives useful insights about how well LLMs cover (or do not cover) low resource languages.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
We are interested in automatically identifying the writing system or script in which a given text is written. We will refer to this automatic identification of scripts as script identification. Script identification is useful when doing research on and developing technology for low resource languages. For example, when compiling a corpus for a low resource language, script identification can serve as part of quality control: texts written in scripts that are not used for the language can be excluded. Similarly, when training the tokenizer of a language model for low resource languages, analyzing the learned token vocabulary lets developers see how well a script is represented, which indicates how well the languages written in that script are represented.

In such low resource scenarios, language identification is an alternative to script identification: it can also be used for quality control and for analyzing language model vocabularies. However, language identification for low resource languages is prone to high error rates [1,2,3]. Many low resource languages are poorly identified by existing tools, due to data scarcity and high variability in orthography, genres and domains. By contrast, script identification can be performed with much higher accuracy, and it is therefore a useful functionality in the absence of reliable language identification for many low resource languages.

In this paper, we present GlotScript, a resource and tool for low resource identification of writing systems, i.e., low resource script identification.

Our contributions are as follows. (i) We compile and organize GlotScript-R, a comprehensive resource for script identification that associates attested writing systems with language varieties, and we make it available to the community. (ii) We publish GlotScript-T, a script identification tool covering all 161 scripts in Unicode 15.0. It computes the script distribution for any input text, with scripts identified by their ISO 15924 codes. To the best of our knowledge, no such tool is currently available. (iii) We demonstrate the benefits of GlotScript-T and GlotScript-R for corpus cleaning, and show that script identification can improve the quality of existing low resource corpora. (iv) We analyze the tokenization of large language models (LLMs), including GPT-4, Falcon and Llama2, using GlotScript-T. This analysis gives valuable insights into LLM coverage (or lack of coverage) of low resource languages.

References:
[1] Kargaran et al. (2023) Amir Hossein Kargaran, Ayyoob Imani, François Yvon, and Hinrich Schütze. 2023. GlotLID: Language identification for low-resource languages . In The 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing .
[2] Kreutzer et al. (2022) Julia Kreutzer, Isaac Caswell, Lisa Wang, Ahsan Wahab, Daan van Esch, Nasanbayar Ulzii-Orshikh, Allahsera Tapo, Nishant Subramani, Artem Sokolov, Claytone Sikasote, et al. 2022. Quality at a glance: An audit of web-crawled multilingual datasets . Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics , 10:50–72.
[3] Caswell et al. (2020) Isaac Caswell, Theresa Breiner, Daan van Esch, and Ankur Bapna. 2020. Language id in the wild: Unexpected challenges on the path to a thousand-language web text corpus. arXiv preprint arXiv:2010.14571 .
